profile: Opens a paragraph on the last paragraph's point, often by naming it: 'Placing the fault in the receiver has two consequences.' / 'Repair is only the start.' / 'The second claim goes further and it is the one this book disputes.'
Ends a paragraph on the point itself, in a short plain sentence that carries the argument, not an ornament: 'In most of us, it is not working.' / 'That side of the religion is called ʿirfan.'

Medium sentences broken by short declaratives; 'and' joins two clauses but never chains three: 'It is not easy and it requires a great deal of training.' Semicolons balance two halves ('God is not withholding signs; we are failing to receive them.'); colons introduce lists ('The signs are all around us: in marriage, in the people we meet…'); 'whereas' appears once.

Names a source once, embeds a short fragment in his own syntax, then restates it plainly: 'There is a machine inside which is [rusted]." That machine is the soul.' Verbs: 'explains', 'insists', 'compares', 'makes the same point', 'accepts'; 'he says' is almost absent.

Verses are introduced by a complete sentence ending in a full stop, then [verse], then an explanation that applies the verse: 'The Qur'an describes the gap in one verse.' Never a claim, a colon and a quotation stacked in one sentence.
Enumerates with 'The first is… The second is…' and signposts other chapters flatly: 'as Chapter One shows', 'Chapter Fourteen sets out their wider concerns'.

Stance is inclusive 'we/us/most of us' and includes the author in the failing: 'Most of us see only the lamp.' Uses 'Let's start with two claims'; 'you' only for the reader's practical use ('words you'll meet'). No lecturing or scolding.
Diction is plain and concrete, argued through homely analogies: red light and lamp, rusted machine, cattle that 'see and hear perfectly well'. No grand or abstract flights.

A stray comma before the main verb after a long subject: 'That something and why it is worth developing, is the subject of this chapter.' / 'The longing for God and the faculty that perceives Him, are part of how we are made.'
Fairness to opposing views stated without heat: 'This claim is not contested.' / 'Where they differ, this book presents each view with neutrality.'

Never uses rhetorical questions, 'So' or 'Indeed' openers, intensifiers, suspense or withheld names, aphoristic antitheses, or a paragraph that only adds a true remark; every paragraph moves one step.

tells: Opens on the preceding point ('Without a chain of authority'), short declaratives, Tabatabaʾi named once and his term explained at once ('He calls him the general teacher: someone who…').
Concrete detail ('which words of remembrance suit that stage'), Author A's stray comma ('what to do next, can lose the way'), and the last line sets up the next step rather than decorating.
'by a judge whose own guide was a weaver no one could identify' — a teaser with withheld names; Author A would point to the box flatly ('The box below gives his training') or name the man

'He is not Mulla ʿAbd al-Samad Hamadani, the Shia ʿarif who found the law, the path and the truth in a single prayer, but another scholar of the same name' — a true aside that does not move the argument; Author A would cut it or leave it to a footnote

'Another gave Imam Khomeini his first formal classes in ethics and gnosis' — lineage detail added for its own sake; the paragraph's point (there are instructors to find) was made two sentences earlier

Verse-introducing sentences are complete and followed by a plain application ('Most of us fear Allah's punishment. The people of this verse fear Him with a fear that is not about punishment at all.'); Sheikh named once.
'These words, he says, belong… He asks why… Telling ordinary believers to say them, he says, is' — 'he says' twice plus 'He asks' in one paragraph; Author A attributes once and then states the point
'The prayers themselves speak from need, as a pupil would' — a loose link that does not answer the difficulty just raised; Author A would say how the prayers answer the Sheikh's objection
'The servant stands there because of need and the prayer gives no other reason for coming' — restates the quotation as a tidy closing line; Author A would stop after the quotation's plain gloss
Opens on the prior step ('If a guide is needed, the next question is what authority he holds'), Sufi position stated fairly before the Shia answer, Sheikh named once and quoted as the conclusion.
Enumerated 'second gift… third gift', verses introduced by full sentences and glossed afterwards, careful note on the translation of shuhadaʾ; 'the fourth is a doorway' moves to the next step.
'for Sheikh Bahmanpour… he says… the ʿurafaʾ say… the Sheikh adds' — four attributions in two short paragraphs; Author A names once and then writes in his own voice
'This light usually reaches a traveller through another heart' — restates the first paragraph's opening ('A light placed in one heart can reach another') instead of advancing
'from heart to heart… from one heart to another… through another heart' — the same image repeated three times where Author A would state it once and apply it

Picks up the reference's last point exactly ('If the faculty can be repaired, there should be people in whom it already works'), concrete gloss after the verse ('a name means little to a person who does not know whom it names').

Kubra named once with his role, quotation glossed plainly ('Their wonders may be real, but their claim to know God is false'); second paragraph picks up the first ('Keeping the law rules a false guide out, but…').
'the Sheikh sets… he says… the Sheikh says… he grants' — four attributions in two paragraphs used as filler; Author A would name him once

'The prophets knew God in this way, with a knowledge present in their hearts and not worked out by argument' — restates the previous paragraph's conclusion ('They wanted a real experience and knowledge of God'); Author A stops once the point is made
'God is not a body and God is not in one place and absent from another' — an 'and' chain; Author A would use a semicolon or two sentences

'It is difficult, but it is open, because we are made for it… He means this as a statement of what we were made for… God created us with that capacity and wants us to reach it' — the same claim three times; Author A says it once
'This is the case for pursuing ʿirfan. The Qur'an invites more than the minimum and…' — a summary paragraph restating the chapter's conclusions; Author A ends on the last step, not a recap
'That rank is open to any believer who obeys God and the Prophet and acts righteously' — tidy closing line; Author A would stop on the preceding point

Plain, concrete information in Author A's flat register ('The Mafatih sets each of them on a night or a day in the believer's year'), each prayer placed in one short sentence, Maliki Tabrizi named once.
'Then: "These are shirk."' — dramatic staging of a quotation; Author A would write 'He calls these shirk' and move on
'Shirk, setting up a partner beside God, is the gravest charge in Islam' — a closing flourish; Author A would stop after the gloss of shirk
'This kind of mysticism must be held apart from the real thing' — a lecturing line that restates the preceding sentence; Author A would go straight to what Islamic mysticism is

Mirrors the reference's chapter opening exactly ('These words come near the end of… The line asks God for…'), with the prayer placed in the believer's week ('when many of us hear it') and a flat recap of the prior chapter.
'a false guide leaves people looking at him and a true guide turns them towards God' — an antithetical aphorism closing the paragraph; Author A would state the test plainly and stop

'Any believer can ask what a person's presence reminds them of, what his speech adds to what they know and what his conduct makes them want' — a polished triple closing line after the point was already made ('Checking them needs no inner sight'); Author A would end there

'The scholars differ in emphasis but agree that powers are not the aim. Mutahhari also explains why seeking them would be shirk: the goal has become something other than God' — a whole paragraph restating what the quotation already said; Author A would cut it
'uses the same word as Sheikh Bahmanpour' — the Sheikh named twice and Mutahhari three times across three short paragraphs; Author A names once and then argues
'consider it "a kind of shirk…" and he recalls Imam ʿAli (as) saying…' — a long quotation joined by 'and' to a second report in one sentence; Author A gives one fragment and glosses it

'Let's start with the two kinds of knowing' echoes the reference's 'Let's start with two claims'; concrete word-lesson ('hadd, also means a limit') with the Sheikh named once and the point then made in Author A's own voice.
